title: Episode 283: Robert H. Goddard: Liquid-Fueled Rocketry, Aunt Effie's Farm, and the Father of Modern Astronautics
description:
The prophetic, solitary, and brilliant life of Dr. Robert Hutchings Goddard: the Worcester physicist and inventor who designed, built, and successfully launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket. Inspired as a boy by H.G. Wells' War of the Worlds while climbing a cherry tree, Goddard dedicated his life to the dream of interplanetary flight. On March 16, 1926, in a snow-covered cabbage patch on Aunt Effie's farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Goddard's slender ten-foot rocket 'Nell' burned liquid oxygen and gasoline, rising forty-one feet in two and a half seconds—an achievement as historic as Kitty Hawk. Mocked by The New York Times as lacking the basic physics of a high school student, Goddard retreated to the desert of Roswell, New Mexico, developing gyroscopic stabilization, steerable thrust, and multistage rocketry. Discover the father of modern astronautics.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series honors the quiet New England visionary whose pioneering liquid-fueled rockets unlocked the path to the stars. Here is George with the extraordinary life of Robert H. Goddard.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CHERRY TREE EPIPHANY OF WORCESTER: 1882 TO 1908
Born in October 1882 in Worcester, Massachusetts, Robert Hutchings Goddard was an only child of Nahum and Fannie Goddard, plagued from early childhood by chronic respiratory illness, pulmonary tuberculosis, and frail health that frequently kept him bedridden for months. Finding solace in his father's brass telescope and the science-fiction novels of Jules Verne and H.G. Wells, young Robert's destiny was crystallized on the sunny afternoon of October 19, 1899. Climbing an old cherry tree in his grandmother's backyard to prune dead branches, seventeen-year-old Robert looked across the fields toward the afternoon sky: 'I imagined how wonderful it would be to make some device which had even the possibility of ascending to Mars... I was a different boy when I came down from that tree.' For the rest of his life, Goddard celebrated October 19 as his personal 'Anniversary Day', dedicating his journals, experiments, and physics studies at Worcester Polytechnic Institute and Clark University to a single, consuming goal: conquering space.  The Goddard family ancestry in Massachusetts reached back to seventeenth-century Puritan settlers, instilling in young Robert an austere New England self-reliance and an unshakeable moral rectitude. Chronic bouts of lung sickness forced him to spend long months confined to bed, where he filled voluminous notebooks with mathematical musings, chemistry formulas, and drawings of futuristic flying machines that could escape Earth's gravitational pull. Climbing that ancient cherry tree behind his grandmother's barn on that crisp October afternoon in 1899, seventeen-year-old Robert felt a mystical communion with the cosmos, experiencing a lightning flash of scientific intuition that convinced him that human destiny lay in reaching across the vast abyss of interplanetary space.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SMITHSONIAN PAPER AND THE MOON ROCKET RIDICULE: 1914 TO 1920
Earning his doctorate in physics from Clark University, Goddard conducted mathematical and laboratory tests proving that rockets could operate efficiently in a vacuum—contrary to the universal belief of contemporary engineers who believed a rocket needed air to push against. In 1914, Goddard secured landmark patents for multi-stage rocketry and liquid-propellant feeding mechanisms. In 1919, the Smithsonian Institution published his modest sixty-nine-page monograph: 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes'. While ninety percent of the paper dealt with atmospheric weather sounding, Goddard included a tiny speculative calculation at the end, suggesting that a multistage rocket loaded with magnesium flash powder could theoretically reach the Moon and ignite a flash visible through telescopes. The press seized on the Moon rocket with sensational mockery: on January 13, 1920, The New York Times published a scathing editorial accusing Goddard of failing to understand the basic laws of physics, asserting that rockets could never fly in the vacuum of space because there was no atmosphere to react against.  Working in the drafty physics laboratory at Clark University, Goddard devised brilliant vacuum-chamber experiments that proved beyond question that rocket engines do not require an external atmosphere to push against, but operate via the pure conservation of momentum expressed in Isaac Newton's third law of motion. His 1919 Smithsonian paper was an architectural masterpiece of mathematical ballistics, calculating nozzle expansions, fuel mass fractions, and staging ratios necessary to achieve escape velocity. The cruel editorial in The New York Times, mocking him as a blundering charlatan who did not understand high school physics, cut Goddard to the soul, prompting him to adopt a lifelong rule of absolute secrecy regarding his experimental breakthroughs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: AUNT EFFIE'S CABBAGE PATCH: MARCH 16, 1926
Deeply wounded by public ridicule, Goddard retreated into secretive isolation, determined to let physical performance answer his critics. Recognizing that solid gunpowder was far too inefficient and explosive for orbital flight, Goddard made the revolutionary decision to develop liquid propellants: liquid oxygen at minus two hundred and ninety-seven degrees Fahrenheit mixed with common motor gasoline. On the freezing morning of March 16, 1926, in a snow-covered cabbage field on his Aunt Effie Ward's farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Goddard erected a slender metal framework holding a ten-foot rocket nicknamed 'Nell'. Standing behind a sheet-metal shield with his wife Esther filming with a hand-cranked camera, Goddard ignited the combustion chamber. The rocket hissed, roared, and leaped forty-one feet into the air, traveling one hundred and eighty-four feet downfield in two and a half seconds before plunging into the frozen cabbage patch. It was the Kitty Hawk of astronautics: the world's very first flight of a liquid-fueled rocket.  The physical layout of the historic March 16, 1926 launch was an astonishing engineering paradox: unlike modern rockets where the motor is at the bottom, Goddard placed the roaring rocket motor at the top of a slender frame, with the gasoline and liquid oxygen tanks trailing below, separated by asbestos heat shields. Igniting the volatile propellants with an alcohol torch on a long pole, Goddard stood frozen with awe as the slender silver tube erupted in white vapor, orange flame, and a deafening roar, shooting into the sky before crashing into the frozen snow. Esther Goddard's iconic photographs of her husband standing in his tweed cap beside the slender metal rocket captured one of the foundational moments in the history of human civilization.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: LINDBERGH'S PATRONAGE AND THE ROSWELL SANCTUARY: 1929 TO 1932
When a noisy July 1929 rocket test in Auburn prompted neighboring villagers to call ambulances and fire engines believing an airplane had crashed, the Massachusetts state fire marshal issued an injunction banning Goddard from launching further rockets in the commonwealth. Fortunately, aviation hero Charles Lindbergh read of the incident and recognized Goddard's genius, flying to Worcester to meet the quiet physicist. Lindbergh secured a massive one-hundred-thousand-dollar philanthropic grant from copper magnate Daniel Guggenheim, enabling Goddard to relocate his laboratory and testing operations to the vast, arid desolation of Roswell, New Mexico. At Mescalero Ranch, surrounded by mesquite and alkali plains, Goddard found the ideal sanctuary: clear skies, open spaces, and freedom from prying eyes.  Charles Lindbergh's sudden arrival at Goddard's Worcester home in November 1929 was an extraordinary act of vision: while the military establishment dismissed Goddard as an eccentric crackpot, the world's most famous aviator immediately recognized that rocketry was the inevitable future of long-range transportation and spaceflight. Lindbergh's personal appeals to philanthropist Daniel Guggenheim secured the essential funding that liberated Goddard from academic teaching burdens, allowing him to establish his machine shops at Mescalero Ranch outside Roswell. In the endless blue skies and silent horizons of the New Mexico desert, Goddard found the ideal physical sanctuary where he could launch roaring multi-stage rockets without police interference or public ridicule.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TECHNICAL BREAKTHROUGHS OF MESCALERO: 1932 TO 1941
In the desert of Roswell, Goddard engineered virtually every foundational technology that powers modern aerospace engineering. He developed gyroscopic steering mechanisms that pivoted small exhaust vanes directly in the rocket plume to maintain vertical flight; he invented centrifugal liquid propellant pumps and regenerative cooling jackets where cold gasoline circulated around the combustion chamber to prevent the metal from melting; and he designed parachute recovery systems to return scientific instruments safely to earth. By the late 1930s, Goddard's rockets were climbing to altitudes of nearly nine thousand feet at speeds exceeding five hundred miles per hour, roaring into the desert sky like roaring silver arrows. Working with a tiny staff of four machinists and his devoted wife Esther, Goddard held over two hundred patents covering the essential architecture of rocketry.  In the isolation of Roswell, Goddard solved virtually every fundamental engineering hurdle of modern astronautics: he invented gyroscopic guidance systems where a small spinning flywheel closed electrical contacts to tilt steering vanes into the exhaust plume, automatically correcting the rocket's flight path in mid-air. He pioneered the lightweight centrifugal turbopumps necessary to inject tons of freezing liquid oxygen and fuel into high-pressure combustion chambers, and developed thin-walled regenerative cooling chambers that prevented engines from burning through their steel walls. When Goddard's twenty-foot rockets roared to altitudes of nearly two miles in the 1930s, deploying silk parachutes to drift gracefully back to the desert floor, he was twenty years ahead of the rest of the scientific world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TRAGIC INDIFFERENCE OF THE PENTAGON AND THE V-2 SHOCK: 1941 TO 1945
As World War Two approached, Goddard offered his rocketry patents and engineering expertise to the United States Army and Navy, urging military leaders to develop long-range ballistic missiles. Tragic shortsightedness blinded American commanders, who relegated the premier rocket scientist in the world to developing small solid-fuel take-off boosters for naval seaplanes at Annapolis. Meanwhile, in Nazi Germany, Wernher von Braun and German engineers eagerly studied Goddard's published papers and American patents, scaling his concepts into the terrifying V-2 rocket that rained supersonic destruction on London in 1944. When captured German V-2 components were brought to Goddard for inspection in 1945, Goddard stared at the gyroscopic vanes, turbopumps, and combustion chambers with quiet, vindicated sorrow, whispering to an assistant: 'They stole them from me.'  The bureaucratic indifference Goddard encountered from American military officials during World War Two was one of the most tragic blunders in military history: Army ordnance officers repeatedly rebuffed his offers to build long-range guided missiles, claiming that rocketry was an impractical fantasy that would play no role in modern combat. German rocket scientists at Peenemünde, led by Wernher von Braun, held no such illusions: they combed through Goddard's American patent files, translating his blueprints directly into the German V-2 rocket that rained supersonic terror upon London. When von Braun surrendered to American forces in 1945, he was asked where he learned how to build liquid-fueled rockets, answering with stunned disbelief: 'Why don't you ask your own Dr. Goddard? We learned everything from him.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF CLARK AND THE RETRACTION OF THE TIMES: 1969 AND BEYOND
Weakened by recurring throat cancer and exhaustion, Robert H. Goddard passed away on August 10, 1945, at age sixty-two, just days before the end of World War Two. In 1960, the United States government officially recognized his intellectual primacy, paying his estate and the Guggenheim Foundation one million dollars for the infringement of his patents. NASA named its premier space research center in Greenbelt, Maryland, the Goddard Space Flight Center in his honor. On July 17, 1969, as Apollo 11 hurtled through the vacuum of cislunar space toward the Moon, The New York Times published a historic editorial correction on page 43, retracting its scathing 1920 editorial: 'Further investigation and experimentation have confirmed the findings of Isaac Newton in the 17th Century and it is now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum... The Times regrets the error.' Robert H. Goddard's cherry tree dream had conquered the stars.  While Goddard died without seeing the fulfillment of his interplanetary dreams, his pioneering blueprints and patents laid the direct technological foundation for the Atlas, Titan, and Saturn rockets that propelled American astronauts into space. On July 17, 1969, as Apollo 11's Saturn V carried Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins toward the Moon, The New York Times' historic retraction of its 1920 editorial served as a poetic, long-delayed vindication of Goddard's lonely genius. Today, the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland directs NASA's most ambitious space telescopes, continuing the sacred mission of the Worcester boy who climbed a cherry tree and dedicated his life to unlocking the boundless heavens for all humanity.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Dr. Robert H. Goddard's lonely brilliance, technical genius, and unyielding faith in the vacuum of space launched the modern space age. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the transformative agricultural miracle of George Washington Carver. Until then, stay curious.
